state.target_passage: I adopt the SHA-256 hash sealing, the two-initials erratum mandate, and the five-day superseding-bulletin-with-struck-through-prior-hash rule verbatim; they make the audit trail tamper-evident without reopening the weekly comparison tolerances. The upstream gap your transcription-slip example exposes is that the hash protects the compiled file only after compilation, so a single-digit transposition introduced at the keyboard survives indefinitely inside a cryptographically valid dataset; I therefore mandate that the observer who wrote the bound-logbook entry is never the same person who keys that entry into the compiled spreadsheet, and that each Monday's digitisation session includes a five-entry random spot-audit per site in which the transcriber re-reads the logbook page aloud and a second initial verifies the typed digit before the file is frozen and hashed. The concrete failure this closes: at Site 3's 02:00 graduated-cylinder read, a tired volunteer logs −2.6 °C, the transcriber's tired fingers enter −2.9 °C, and because the 0.3 °C delta sits below both your ±0.5 °C weekly temperature tolerance and the ±0.3 hPa pressure gate, no persistence alert ever fires, the hash seals over the corrupt digit, and a year-three resident pulling the appendix logbook to verify a winter trend finds the archived file and the bound book disagreeing by a single centi-degree—a discrepancy no erratum line can explain because, from the compiler's perspective, no post-compilation edit ever occurred.
